title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 366
paragraphs: The twelve kings continued to rule justly, but in the course of time the following happened. After sacrificing in the temple of Hephaistos, they were about to make a libation on the last day of the festival, and the chief priest, bringing out for them the golden cups they customarily used to pour libations, miscounted and brought out only eleven for the twelve kings. Then the one standing last in order, Psammetichos, since he had no cup, took off his bronze helmet, and holding it out to receive the wine, he proceeded to make his libation. Likewise all the other kings were accustomed to wear helmets, and they happened to have them on at that moment. Now Psammetichos held out his helmet with no treacherous intent; but they, noting what Psammetichos had done and recalling the oracle — how it had been declared to them that whichever of them should pour a libation with a bronze cup would be sole king of Egypt — remembering, I say, the saying of the oracle, did not indeed think it right to kill Psammetichos, since they found on inquiry that he had not done it with any premeditation. But they decided to strip him of almost all his power and to drive him away into the marshland, and that from the marshland he should have no dealings with the rest of Egypt.
